replication.target_description: Relationship between financial communication and financial disagreements.; multiple cross-sectional standardized actor/partner paths at pp. 2536–2537 and longitudinal alternatives pp. 2538–2539; unresolved row correspondence.

n.sample_role: Candidate only: 1,079 mixed-gender newlywed dyads in each SEM; row correspondence unresolved.
n.exclusions: Continuously married W1–W5; 34 same-gender dyads excluded; FIML for missing data.
n.location: p. 2532, Data and sample; p. 2537 Figure 1; p. 2539 Figure 2
n.quote:
For these reasons, we removed the 34 same-gender couples from our study, which yielded a
final analytical sample of 1,079 mixed-gender, newlywed dyads. ... The standardized, cross-sectional, actor–partner associations (N = 1,079 newlywed couples). ... The standardized, longitudinal, actor–partner associations (N = 1,079 newlywed couples).

es.location: p. 2537 (PDF p. 11), Direct effects/Figure 1; pp. 2538–2539, longitudinal results/Figure 2
es.quote:
Similarly, wives’ healthy financial communication simultaneously predicted
their own financial disagreements (β = .42; p < .001; medium effect size) and their husbands’
(β = .16; p < .001; small effect size) financial disagreements. ... Likewise, husbands’ healthy financial com-
munication simultaneously predicted fewer financial disagreements from their own perspective
(β = .41; p < .001; medium effect size) and their spouse’s perspective (β = .19; p < .001;
small effect size).

reported_success.quote:
H1a and H2a were mostly supported. ... H1b and H2b were not supported. ... These findings suggest that whereas husbands’ healthy financial communica-
tion predicts changes in their own marital satisfaction, their own financial disagreements, and
wives’ financial disagreements, wives’ healthy financial communication only predicted changes
in their own perception of financial disagreements.

notes: Assigned description and pp. 10–11 locator do not identify predictor spouse, outcome spouse, or actor versus partner path. Two assigned rows have the identical description and locator; their order supplies no identity evidence. The locator favors the cross-sectional model but still leaves four direct candidate paths. No candidate is assigned to this audit_id. Cross-sectional Figure 1, p. 2537 (PDF p. 11), standardized direct coefficients: wives communication -> own disagreements beta −.42, p < .001; wives -> husbands disagreements beta −.16, p < .001; husbands -> own disagreements beta −.41, p < .001; husbands -> wives disagreements beta −.19, p < .001. Longitudinal p. 2538 (PDF p. 12), Figure 2 p. 2539 (PDF p. 13): husbands W4 communication -> own W5 disagreements beta −.22, p < .001; husbands -> wives disagreements beta −.10, p < .01; wives -> own disagreements beta −.12, p < .01; wives -> husbands depicted as nonsignificant without numerical coefficient. Metric standardization is explicit in Figure 1 and Figure 2 captions; coefficients are not converted. PDF pp. 11–13 rendered and visually inspected. The canonical text drops minus signs in disagreement coefficients; negative signs above are verified visually in the PDF, while all evidence quotes preserve canonical text exactly. Existing PDF highlights were not used to map rows. Model N candidate: 1,079 newlywed dyads, not 1,079 independent individual participants; stated directly for both models, no sum performed. Inclusion required continuous marriage W1–W5; excluded 34 same-gender dyads from 1,113 intact dyads. FIML used for missing data (Data analysis p. 2535); no complete-case N inferred. Common N retained only as candidate for field-scope review because row correspondence is unresolved. Reported-success hypotheses refer to indirect paths and differ by model; no row-specific narrative verdict assigned. Original side is an unassigned placeholder, not a finding about original source availability.
